hmmt-feb-2007-geo-01.title: Set up the equation
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-01.body:
The surface area is $6s^2$, the volume $s^3$, so $6s^2=s^3+5s$. Since $s>0$, divide by $s$: $s^2-6s+5=0$, i.e. $(s-1)(s-5)=0$.

**Answer: $s=1$ or $s=5$**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-02.title: Power of a point
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-02.body:
Let $BP=x$, so $PD=6-x$. Then $AP\cdot PC=BP\cdot PD$ gives $8=x(6-x)$, so $x^2-6x+8=0$ and $x=2$ or $x=4$. Since $BP<DP$, $x<3$, so $BP=2$.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-03.title: Triangle $MNO$ is equilateral
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-03.body:
$ABC$ is the contact triangle of $MNO$ (its vertices are the tangency points). It is equilateral only if $MNO$ is equilateral, so the three circles are congruent with radius $r$, $MN=NO=OM=2r$, and $ABC$ is the medial triangle of $MNO$ with side $r$. Hence $r=1$ and $MNO$ has side $2$.

**Coordinates.** $M=(0,0)$, $N=(2,0)$, $O=(1,\sqrt3)$, all radii $1$. Then $A=\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)$, $P=O+(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)=\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2\right)$ and $Q=M-(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)=\left(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. Line $AP$ is $x=\frac32$; it meets $\omega_2$ (centre $(2,0)$, radius $1$) at $y=\pm\frac{\sqrt3}2$, so $R=\left(\tfrac32,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)$. Triangle $PQR$ has the vertical side $PR=2\sqrt3$ and $Q$ is at horizontal distance $2$ from line $PR$, so $$[PQR]=\tfrac12\cdot2\sqrt3\cdot2=2\sqrt3.$$

**Answer: $2\sqrt3$**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-04.title: Equal tangent lengths
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-04.body:
Let $T_1,T_2,T_3$ be the points where $AB$, $AC$, $BC$ touch $\omega$. Because $\omega$ lies outside triangle $ABC$ (it is the $A$-excircle), $BT_3=BT_1$ and $CT_3=CT_2$ with $T_3$ between $B$ and $C$, so $BT_1+CT_2=BC=7$. Also $AT_1=AT_2=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=12$. Thus $24=AT_1+AT_2=(AB+BT_1)+(AC+CT_2)=AB+AC+7$, so $AB+AC=17$.

**Answer: 17**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-05.title: Radii form a geometric progression
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-05.body:
Let the half-angle of the cone be $\theta$. A marble of radius $r$ touching the wall has its centre on the axis at distance $r/\sin\theta$ from the apex. Two consecutive marbles with radii $r<r'$ touch each other, so the distance between centres is $r+r'$: $$\frac{r'-r}{\sin\theta}=r+r'\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{r'}{r}=\frac{1+\sin\theta}{1-\sin\theta},$$ a constant. So the five radii form a geometric progression, and the middle one is the geometric mean of the ends: $\sqrt{8\cdot18}=12$.

**Answer: 12**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-06.title: Find the triangle, then power of a point
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-06.body:
Let $AB=c$, $AC=b$: $bc=300$, $b^2+c^2=625$, so $(b+c)^2=1225$, $b+c=35$ and $\{b,c\}=\{15,20\}$; since $AB>AC$, $AB=20$, $AC=15$. The inradius is $r=\frac{b+c-25}2=5$. The incircle touches $AC$ at $M$ and $AB$ at $N$, with $AM=AN=r=5$ (the centre, $A$, $M$, $N$ form a square). So $BN=20-5=15$ and $BM=\sqrt{AB^2+AM^2}=\sqrt{400+25}=5\sqrt{17}$. Power of the point $B$: $BL\cdot BM=BN^2=225$, so $$BL=\frac{225}{5\sqrt{17}}=\frac{45}{\sqrt{17}}=\frac{45\sqrt{17}}{17}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{45\sqrt{17}}{17}$**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-07.title: Cyclic quadrilateral and Ptolemy
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-07.body:
Triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with apex angle $60^\circ$, hence equilateral and $AC=7$. In triangle $ACD$, $\cos\angle ADC=\dfrac{3^2+5^2-7^2}{2\cdot3\cdot5}=-\dfrac12$, so $\angle ADC=120^\circ=180^\circ-\angle ABC$. Thus $ABCD$ is cyclic. Ptolemy: $AC\cdot BD=AB\cdot CD+AD\cdot BC$, i.e. $7\,BD=7\cdot5+3\cdot7$, so $BD=8$.

**Answer: 8**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-08.title: $ABCD$ is cyclic
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-08.body:
Reflect $B$ in line $AC$ to $B'$; since $AC$ bisects $\angle BAD$ and $AB<AD$, $B'$ lies on segment $AD$, with $CB'=CB=CD$ and $\angle AB'C=\angle ABC$. Triangle $CB'D$ is isosceles, so $\angle CDA=\angle CB'D=180^\circ-\angle AB'C=180^\circ-\angle ABC$. Hence $ABCD$ is cyclic.

Angle chase: $\angle CBD=\angle CAD=20^\circ$ and, in triangle $ABD$, $\angle ADB=180^\circ-40^\circ-130^\circ=10^\circ$. Since $CB=CD$, $\angle CDB=\angle CBD=20^\circ$, so $\angle ADC=\angle ADB+\angle BDC=10^\circ+20^\circ=30^\circ$. In isosceles triangle $CDE$ ($DC=DE$) with apex angle $30^\circ$, $\angle DEC=75^\circ$, so $\angle AEC=105^\circ$, and in triangle $AEC$: $\angle ACE=180^\circ-20^\circ-105^\circ=55^\circ$.

**Answer: $55^\circ$**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-09.title: Trigonometry
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-09.body:
Let $AD=x$ and $\angle ABC=t$. Then $AB=1+x$ and in right triangle $ABE$, $\cos t=\dfrac{BE}{AB}=\dfrac1{1+x}$. Since $BD=CD=1$, triangle $BDC$ is isosceles with $\angle DCB=\angle DBC=t$, so $\angle DCA=(90^\circ-t)-t=90^\circ-2t$ and $\angle ADC=2t$. In right triangle $ADC$ (right angle at $A$), $\cos2t=\dfrac{AD}{CD}=x$. Then $2\cos^2t-1=x$ gives $\dfrac2{(1+x)^2}=1+x$, so $(1+x)^3=2$ and $x=\sqrt[3]2-1$.

**Answer: $\sqrt[3]{2}-1$**

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-09.title: Similar triangles
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-09.body: Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Then $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle EBA\sim\triangle MBD$ ($D$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ since $DB=DC$). So $AB^2=BC\cdot BE=BC$, and $\frac{BM}{BD}=\frac{AB}{BC}$ i.e. $\frac{BC/2}{1}=\frac{AB}{BC}$, so $BC^2=2AB$. With $BC=AB^2$ this gives $AB^4=2AB$, $AB=\sqrt[3]2$ and $AD=AB-1=\sqrt[3]2-1$.

hmmt-feb-2007-geo-10.title: Area two ways
hmmt-feb-2007-geo-10.body:
$AC^2=AB^2+BC^2=13$ and $CD^2-DA^2=49-36=13$, so $\angle DAC=90^\circ$. Therefore $$[ABCD]=[ABC]+[DAC]=\tfrac12\cdot2\cdot3+\tfrac12\cdot6\sqrt{13}=3+3\sqrt{13}.$$ With incenter $I$ and inradius $r$, $[ABCD]=\tfrac r2(AB+BC+CD+DA)=\tfrac r2\cdot18=9r$ (the sides have total $2+3+7+6=18$; note $AB+CD=BC+DA=9$, consistent with an incircle). So $r=\dfrac{3+3\sqrt{13}}9=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{13}}3$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{1+\sqrt{13}}3$**
